newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - German SPD split wide open on EMU timetable.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - German SPD split wide open on EMU timetable.

text.p: A wide difference of opinion on whether Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU) should be delayed emerged within the top leadership of Germany's main opposition Social Democratic (SPD) party on Wednesday.

The split became clear after a poll published earlier this week showed that the party rank-and-file was divided on the issue, raising questions about the party's official line on EMU ahead of elections due next year.

Gerhard Schroeder, a leading Social Democrat potential candidate for chancellor, was quoted in an article as saying he believed it would be better to delay the launch of Europe's planned single currency than to soften the criteria.

"I would see that as less bad than to ignore the criteria and give up the stability orientation," Schroeder, whom opinion polls place above Chancellor Helmut Kohl in terms of personal popularity, said in an interview with Die Zeit weekly.
Speaking in the Bild mass circulation daily newspaper, however, Schroeder's party chief Oskar Lafontaine came out with exactly the opposite line.

"Despite all the problems, I am in favour of launching the euro in 1999," Lafontaine said. "The government has done everything to put up unnecessary hurdles. The overly-tight interpretation of the Maastricht criteria has damaged the process of the monetary union."

The divergence of views reflects the ideological distance between the two men, with Schroeder generally seen as on the party's right-wing and more amenable to the economic reforms and state spending cuts Bonn is seeking to introduce.

That these reforms, whether on tax, pensions or welfare provision, remain mostly incomplete is widely linked to the opposition of Lafontaine's wing of the party and its resistance to what it sees as pre-EMU attacks on Germany's welfare state.

According to a survey of 1,400 SPD members published by the news magazine Der Spiegel this week, 40 percent would like to see EMU made an issue at next year's general elections, with 59 percent resisting such a strategy.

Of those who would like to make it an issue, however, a high 78 percent said they backed a postponement of EMU, suggesting that a sizeable minority of the party would like it to run on an "EMU-delay" ticket.
That could be a risky strategy with German voters. While recent polls show most want a delay of EMU, the majority have also firmly indicated they do not want to see it as an election issue.
